solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Call for skin treatment

blocks.note: first meaning: the evening drum or bugle signal calling soldiers back to quarters
second meaning: a permanent inked design on the skin

explanation.surface: Someone shouts out for a skin-care session at a salon.
explanation.walkthrough: The military sense is the less familiar one: a tattoo was the signal recalling troops at night, hence also a military display.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a military evening signal summoning soldiers and an inked design put permanently into a person's body.

clue.text: Hospital units in the county

blocks.note: first meaning: hospital capacity is counted in places for patients to lie
second meaning: the short form of Bedfordshire, an English county

explanation.surface: A report on how many hospital wards there are in a particular county.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedfordshire, a county north of London, is commonly shortened to Beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospitals measure their capacity in places for patients to sleep, and the same letters abbreviate an English county name.

clue.text: Aesthetic writer in a depression after the end of year

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the depression is placed behind the preceding letters

blocks.note: December closes the year; DEC is its calendar abbreviation
taken as written
a dent is a small hollow

explanation.surface: A poet of the aesthetic movement sinks into gloom as the year closes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a depression' reads as the writer's mood, but 'in' only links the definition, and the depression is a literal hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Decadents were late nineteenth-century writers of the aesthetic movement, such as Wilde and Verlaine, so one of them is an aesthetic writer.

clue.text: Port? A distinguished artist drinks unit much less than litre

indicators.note: a drinker takes liquid inside, so the artist takes the tiny unit into himself

blocks.note: an Associate of the Royal Academy
a cubic centimetre is a thousandth of a litre

explanation.surface: A famous painter in a harbour town sips only the tiniest measure of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: ARA, Associate of the Royal Academy, is a British painter's honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital of Ghana and a seaport on the Gulf of Guinea, so it is a port.

clue.text: A beautiful person crossing my French carpet

indicators.note: the beautiful person stretches across and so straddles the French word

blocks.note: taken as written
a dish is slang for an attractive person
the French word for my

explanation.surface: A good-looking person walks across a rug that belongs to a French speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a floor covering but is the verb: to carpet someone is to reprimand them.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is British slang for calling them in to be reprimanded, which is to scold or rebuke them.

clue.text: Make sense of counters in the wrong order

indicators.note: letters set in a wrong order must be rearranged to find the right one

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tries to understand why the board-game pieces have been set out jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To construe a statement is to interpret it, working out its meaning.

clue.text: Worker maybe with achievement meeting Queen – one of her guards

blocks.note: a worker bee; 'maybe' marks it as an example
a feat is a notable achievement
Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: An accomplished worker gets to meet the Queen and joins her guard.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beefeaters are the Yeoman Warders of the Tower of London, part of the sovereign's ceremonial bodyguard.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefeaters are the royal Yeomen of the Guard and Tower warders, so one is a guard of the Queen.

clue.text: Undergarment – one slipping down a little in restaurant

indicators.note: one letter slides a short way along the word, rearranging the undergarment's letters slightly

blocks.note: the full name of a bra

explanation.surface: A bra strap slips a little while someone is dining out.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the I (one) moves: it slides two places further along the word, past the E and R, to give BRASSERIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A brasserie is an informal French-style restaurant serving food and drink.

clue.text: End story in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience hears things, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: The end of a narrative performed in a theatre hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The tail is the rear end of something, as in the tail of a queue.

clue.text: Managed to get man on board, creating a row

blocks.note: ran a business means managed it
the king, a chess piece, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Someone got a man aboard a ship and started a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it means a line; 'board' is a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank is a line of people or things side by side, as in a taxi rank or soldiers in rank.

clue.text: One enthusiast in the end reversing trivial little thing

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so the word for the end is read back to front
the one enthusiast sits inside the other word, enclosed by it

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a fitness nut is a fan
an end is a goal

explanation.surface: A fan is finally reversing direction on some small trivial point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end' means a goal or purpose here, not a finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A minutia is a tiny or trivial detail, normally seen in the plural minutiae.

clue.text: Place offering type of drug, nothing for swallowing

indicators.note: something swallowed ends up inside, so the drug takes nothing within it

blocks.note: statins are cholesterol-lowering drugs
zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A pharmacy offers a kind of medicine and nothing else to take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For swallowing' looks like how a pill is taken, but it tells you the drug takes in the nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A station is a post or position, the place where someone is set to stand.

clue.text: Independent country? There’s attention as that falls apart

indicators.note: something that falls apart breaks up, so its letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A new country wins notice just as the old one collapses.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation state is a sovereign country whose people largely share one national identity, so it is self-governing.

clue.text: An inspiration to Isaac – and it makes Peter leap about

indicators.note: leaping about means jumping around, so the letters are moved around into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that inspired Isaac also sends Peter jumping around.
explanation.walkthrough: Isaac is Isaac Newton, said to have thought of gravity on seeing fruit fall from a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says a falling fruit from one of these in his garden inspired Newton's theory of gravity.

clue.text: I hurry after maiden – some sort of mistake

indicators.note: the I and the hurry come after the maiden, so they follow it in sequence

blocks.note: M is a maiden over in cricket scoring
taken as written
to sprint is to run fast

explanation.surface: Someone rushes after a young woman, and it proves to be some kind of blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden is a cricket over with no runs, written M on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a typographical error in printed text, one kind of mistake.

clue.text: Finish up being hugged by good girl? That brings contentment

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
what is hugged is held inside someone's arms, so it sits within the other letters

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a lass is a girl
a finish is an end

explanation.surface: Ending up hugged by a nice girl makes for a happy feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' turns the word around; G and LASS together then wrap round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladness is happiness or pleasure, close in sense to a state of satisfaction and content.

clue.text: Request to keep quiet, say – something used to keep folk in the dark?

definitions.text: something used to keep folk in the dark

blocks.note: the hushing sound
to say is to speak

explanation.surface: Hushing someone up is a way of keeping people uninformed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the dark' suggests secrecy, but it is literal: a window covering blocks the light.
explanation.definitionFit: A shutter is a hinged panel closed over a window to block out daylight from a room.

clue.text: One who helps others to succeed?

definitions.text: One who helps others to succeed?

blocks.clueFragment: One who helps others to succeed?
blocks.note: surface reading: a mentor or coach who helps people do well
setter's reading: succeed means inherit, so this is someone whose will lets heirs take over property

explanation.walkthrough: Succeed here means to come into an inheritance, not to do well.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator makes a will, so on death the named heirs succeed to the estate and possessions.

clue.text: Old man facing test to become a legal immigrant

indicators.note: the old man stands in front of the test, so comes first in the sequence

blocks.note: pa is a father
a trial is a test

explanation.surface: An elderly father faces an exam to gain lawful residence.
explanation.walkthrough: Patrial was a British legal term for someone with a right of abode in the UK through a parent or grandparent.
explanation.definitionFit: Under British immigration law a patrial had the right to settle in the UK by ancestry, so was a lawful incomer.

clue.text: Dopey setter, awfully unimaginative?

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The compiler mocks himself as a dull, unoriginal fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Stereotyped means fixed and conventional, lacking originality, as in formulaic thinking.

clue.text: Drunk beginning to shed items of clothing

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: tight is slang for drunk
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A tipsy person starts taking off garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Tights are close-fitting legwear covering the hips and legs, worn as clothing.

clue.text: Racecourse expelling a fellow wearing a kilt?

indicators.note: expelling means throwing out, so a letter is removed from the racecourse

blocks.note: Ascot is a famous English racecourse
taken as written

explanation.surface: A racecourse throws out a man dressed in Highland garb.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot, in Berkshire, hosts Royal Ascot; take its A away.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilt is traditional Highland dress, so a man in one is likely a Scotsman; the question mark admits it is only an example.

clue.text: Island visible to all with school of whales around it

indicators.note: the whales are placed around, so they surround and enclose the other letter

blocks.note: a gam is a school of whales
U is the universal film certificate

explanation.surface: An island can be seen by everyone with whales swimming around it.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for all audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: Guam is a Pacific island in the Marianas, a United States territory.

clue.text: Running some university rave – a hundred going to it

indicators.note: the hundred goes onto the rest, joining it at the front of the sequence

blocks.note: Roman numeral
the Open University
to rave is to rant

explanation.surface: A university party is running, with a hundred people heading there.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university, abbreviated OU.
explanation.definitionFit: Courant is a heraldic term describing an animal shown in the act of running.

clue.text: Holiday accident?

blocks.note: first meaning: a journey or outing
second meaning: a stumble or fall

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a single mishap while away; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a short journey taken for pleasure and a stumble over something underfoot.

clue.text: I’m great playing jazzy music

indicators.note: playing with something means fiddling around with it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boastful pianist praises himself while performing syncopated tunes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragtime is syncopated piano music popular around 1900, a forerunner of jazz.

clue.text: Time to get up? Avoid making a commitment for a while

definitions.text: Avoid making a commitment for a while

blocks.note: tempo is musical time
to rise is to get out of bed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is morning, while dodging any firm promise.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to stall or be evasive in order to gain time before deciding.

clue.text: Groan as one receiving letter from Paul

blocks.note: first meaning: ... Groan, hero of Mervyn Peake's Gormenghast novels
second meaning: the companion to whom Saint Paul addressed a New Testament epistle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Groan' looks like a moan, but it is a surname: Titus Groan is the first Gormenghast novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Peake's young earl is called Titus Groan, and the Pauline Epistle to Titus was written to Paul's disciple of that name.
